QUESTIONS PRESENTED
1. Whether the NVRA or a federal consent  judgment prohibits Arizona from rejecting voter registration applications from applicants who submit a state
voter registration form without documentary proof of
citizenship, rather than registering such voters as federal-only voters, as it would if they submitted a federal voter registration form without documentary
proof of citizenship.
2. Whether the NVRA ’s restriction on “any program” that “systematically” removes voters from the
rolls from continuing in the 90 days leading up to  a
federal election requires  Arizona to pause  its database-driven program to remove suspected noncitizens
from the rolls.

INTRODUCTION
This case concerns two provisions in the National
Voter Registration Act (NVRA) that protect the rights
of eligible voters to vote in federal elections. The first
requires state -created voter registration forms , like
the federal voter registration form, to ask for no more
information than “necessary” when used to  register
voters for federal elections.  The second requires
States to pause “any program” “to systematically remove the names of ineligible voters” from the rolls
during the 90 days before federal elections, except at
the voter’s request, due to a criminal con viction or
mental incapacity finding, or due to the voter’s death.
The Ninth Circuit correctly held that the challenged features of Arizona election law are preempted
by these provisions. The first provision preempts Arizona’s rule that applicants  who submit a state voter
registration form will have their application rejected
entirely if they do not include  documentary proof of
citizenship, even for federal elections  where the
NVRA controls . Petitioners1 never established that
documentary proof of citizenship is “necessary” under
those circumstances. This Court held in Arizona v. Inter Tribal Council of Arizona, Inc. , 570 U.S. 1 (2013)
(“ITCA”), that the NVRA prohibits  Arizona from requiring applicants using the federal voter registration
form to provide documentary proof of citizenship, and

1 “Petitioners” collectively refers to the Republican National
Committee (RNC) as well as the United States, the State of Arizona, Arizona Attorney General Kristin K. Mayes, Warren Peterson, and Steve Montenegro.

2


the Election Assistance Commission (EAC) has never
found such a requirement “necessary” as would be required to add it to  the federal form.  52 U.S.C.
§ 20508(b)(1); see Kobach v. U.S. Election Assistance
Comm’n, 772 F.3d 1183 (10th Cir. 2014), cert. denied,
576 U.S. 1055 (2015). The identical “necessary” standard governs the state form, too, when used to register
for federal elections. 52 U.S.C. § 20505(a)(2). And the
entire structure of the NVRA’s mail registration provisions reflects Congress’s determination that providing information on a form and attesting to its accuracy
is sufficient for federal voter registration, and that
States can demand more only if they show that doing
so is necessary.
The second provision partially preempts Arizona’s
requirement that election officials compare the voter
rolls against various databases every month and initiate a process to remove voters who are flagged as
possible noncitizens in those databases, even where
such comparisons would occur within the 90 days preceding a federal election. Petitioners misunderstand
the purpose of this provision, which is intended to protect eligible voters against erroneous removal on the
cusp of an election—a danger that fully applies to systematic removals of suspected noncitizens. Indeed, recent history is littered with examples of naturalized
citizens being wrongly labeled as noncitizens by systematic reviews. Petitioners’ argument that the
NVRA must be interpreted to allow systematic removals of suspected noncitizens within the quiet period or
else noncitizens could never  be removed is simply
wrong—the general removal prohibition uses a different and potentially narrower term, “registrant[s],”

3


whereas the quiet -period provision refers more
broadly to all systematic removals of “ineligible voters.” See 52 U.S.C. § 20507(a)(3), (c)(2)(A).
The NVRA reflects Congress’s careful balance between facilitating voter registration and electoral participation on the one hand, and promoting accurate
voter rolls on the other. See Husted v. A. Philip Randolph Inst., 584 U.S. 756, 761 (2018). Congress’s calibration of those “competing values” is “the very essence of legislative choice.” Rodriguez v. United
States, 480 U.S. 522, 526 (1987) (per curiam). The job
of the courts is to “take care not to undo” Congress’s
work. King v. Burwell, 576 U.S. 473, 498 (2015). The
Ninth Circuit appropriately respected the balance
struck by Congress by applying the NVRA’s plain language to Arizona’s election laws. This Court should affirm.
STATEMENT
I. The National Voter Registration Act
The NVRA “erect[s] a complex superstructure of
federal regulation atop state voter -registration systems.” ITCA, 570 U.S. at 5. Congress erected this federal overlay because “the right of citizens of the
United States to vote is a fundamental right,” and “it
is the duty of the Federal, State, and local governments to promote the exercise of that right.” 52 U.S.C.
§ 20501(a)(1)–(2). Congress therefore crafted the
NVRA to “increase the number of eligible citizens who
register to vote in elections for Federal office” and to
“enhance[] the participation of eligible citizens as voters in elections for Federal office.” Id. § 20501(b)(1)–

4


(2). To do so, Congress, among other things, “requir[ed] States to provide simplified systems for registering to vote in federal elections.” ITCA, 570 U.S. at
5 (quoting Young v. Fordice, 520 U.S. 273, 275 (1997)).
In addition to promoting access to voting, the
NVRA was also crafted to “protect the integrity of the
electoral process” and “ensure that accurate and current voter registration rolls are maintained.” 52
U.S.C. §  20501(b)(3)–(4). Congress struck a “careful
balance” between those “competing purposes” by, for
example, permitting States to use systematic programs to remove ineligible voters from the rolls, while
also prohibiting those systematic programs close to an
election. Arcia v. Fla. Sec’y of State, 772 F.3d 1335,
1346 (11th Cir. 2014).
1. The NVRA generally supplies two paths for registering to vote in federal elections, both of which are
relevant here. First, the NVRA requires that States
“shall accept and use” a federal voter -registration
form developed by the EAC “for the registration of voters in elections for Federal office.” 52 U.S.C.
§ 20505(a)(1); see also id. § 20508(a)(2). Second, the
NVRA permits States to “develop and use” their own
state voter registration forms as an alternative to the
federal form, id.  § 20505(a)(2). State forms that are
used for registration to vote in federal elections are
subject to many of the same requirements as the federal form, including that they “may require only such
identifying information . . . as is necessary to enable
the appropriate State election official to assess the eligibility of the applicant,” id. § 20508(b)(1). The NVRA
also requires public assistance agencies to distribute

5


the federal form to applicants for public assistance or,
alternatively, a state form that is “equivalent” to the
federal form. Id. § 20506(a)(6).
2. The NVRA also imposes requirements and limitations related to “removing ineligible persons” from
the voter rolls. Husted, 584 U.S. at 761. As relevant
here, States “shall complete, not later than 90 days
prior to the date of a primary or general election for
Federal office, any program the purpose of which is to
systematically remove the names of ineligible voters
from the official lists of eligible voters.” 52 U.S.C.
§ 20507(c)(2)(A) (emphasis added). A separate provision provides that, at all times, a “registrant” may “not
be removed” from the voter rolls except at the registrant’s request, due to a criminal conviction or finding
of mental incapacity, due to death, or due to a change
of residence. Id. § 20507(a)(3).
II. Arizona’s Bifurcated Voter Registration
System After ITCA
In 2004, Arizona enacted a law requiring election
officials to “reject any application for registration” —
including the federal form—“that is not accompanied”
by documentary proof of citizenship, such as a U.S.
passport or birth certificate. A.R.S. §  16-166(F). In
ITCA, the Court held the NVRA preempts that requirement as to the federal form. See 570 U.S. at 6 –
10. The Court explained that as a “straightforward
textual” matter, the NVRA “mandate[s] that Arizona
‘accept and use’ the Federal Form” as prepared by the
EAC and does not allow Arizona to add additional requirements like documentary proof o f citizenship. Id.
at 9. And after the Court held that Arizona could ask

6


the EAC to add such a requirement to the federal
form, the Commission declined that request, a decision that the Tenth Circuit affirmed and this Court
declined to review. See Kobach, 772 F.3d 1183.
Unable to add the requirement to the federal form,
Arizona continued to require documentary proof of citizenship from applicants to vote in state and local elections. After ITCA, however, Arizona created a second,
“federal-only” tier of voter registration for voters who
submit a federal voter registration form without documentary proof of citizenship. Such “federal-only” voters may vote only in federal elections and not for state
and local offices. A.R.S. § 16-127.
In adopting this two-tier system, Arizona initially
allowed only applicants who used the federal form ,
and did not provide documentary proof of citizenship,
to be registered as federal- only voters; registrants
who submitted a state  form without documentary
proof of citizenship had their registrations rejected
outright. App.18a–19a. Arizona also registered federal form applicants as full voters if county officials
could locate proof of citizenship on file with a state
agency, while denying that privilege to state form applicants. See App.19a, 193a–94a, 402a.
In 2017, however,  the League of United Latin
American Citizens of Arizona and other organizations
sued to challenge that disparate treatment, alleging
that Arizona’s “arbitrary dual voter registration policies . . . irrationally disenfranchise thousands of eligible Arizona voters” based on the registration form
they happened to use. Complaint  ¶ 1, League of
United Latin American Citizens of Arizona v. Reagan,

7


No. 2:17-CV-4102-PHX-DGC (D. Ariz. Nov. 11, 2017),
ECF No. 1. Plaintiffs brought claims under the First
and Fourteenth Amendments to the U.S. Constitution
and named as defendants Arizona’s Secretary of State
and the Maricopa County Recorder. After filing responsive pleadings , the Secretary and Maricopa
County Recorder entered into a consent decree ( the
“LULAC Consent Decree”) to resolve the litigation.
See App.474a–94a. The LULAC Consent Decree ,
among other things, obliged the Secretary to instruct
Arizona’s county recorders to treat f ederal form and
state form applicants similarly . It required that, f or
registrants who did not submit documentary proof of
citizenship alongside an application, county recorders
first check to see if the applicant previously submitted
such documentation to the Motor Vehicle Department
(MVD). If so, the applicant would be  registered as a
full-ballot voter, regardless of form submitted . If not
located, however, such applicants would be registered
as federal-only voters—again regardless of the form
submitted. That remained Arizona’s practice until the
enactment of H.B. 2492.
III. H.B. 2492’s Documentary Proof of Citizenship Requirements
In early 2022, Arizona enacted H.B. 2492. The law
requires that registrants who submit a state form
without documentary proof of citizenship be rejected
outright, rather than be registered as federal-only voters. See A.R.S. §  16-121.01(C)–(D). This “state -form
rejection” provision sought to restore Arizona’s differential treatment of federal form and state form applicants, notwithstanding the LULAC Consent Decree,

8


which H.B. 2492 did not mention or acknowledge in
any manner.
IV. H.B. 2243’s Cancellation Provision
In tandem, Arizona passed H.B. 2243, which requires officials to conduct citizenship checks  “each
month” of all the voters on its rolls, with additional
checks for federal-only voters and voters who officials
have “reason to believe” are not U.S. citizens. A.R.S.
§ 16-165(G)–(K). This review is based on  cross-referencing the rolls with various local, state, and federal
databases. See id. County recorders must then send
flagged voters a notice that their registrations will be
canceled in 35 days if they do not provide “satisfactory
evidence of United States citizenship .” Id. § 16-
165(A)(10).
V. The Present Litigation
On March 31, 2022, Mi Familia Vota and Voto Latino sued Arizona’s Secretary of State, Attorney General, and county recorders to enjoin enforcement of
certain provisions in the newly enacted laws .
App.344a. The United States and other organizational
plaintiffs soon filed their own suits , and the various
suits were ultimately consolidated. App.344a . The
RNC and the Petersen  Petitioners (the Arizona Senate President and House Speaker ) intervened as defendants. None of the defendants or intervenors ever
sought to modify or set aside the LULAC Consent Decree.
The district court resolved the claims at issue here
in a September 2023 summary judgment order.

9


App.336a–84a. As relevant to the issues Petitioner s
raise here, t he court held that Arizona could not enforce the state -form rejection provision because the
LULAC Consent Decree “ha[d] never [been] set aside”
and it therefore prohibited “precisely the conduct”
mandated by H.B. 2492. App.36 5a–66a. In the alternative, t he court held that  the state -form rejection
provision was preempted by the NVRA. App.366a
n.13. The court also held that the systematic removal
program mandated by H.B. 2243 violated the NVRA’s
prohibition against systematic removals of voters
within 90 days of a federal election. App.357a–60a.
In December 2023, the court held a 10 -day bench
trial to address other outstanding claims. App.23a. On
May 2, 2024, the court entered a final judgment that
granted permanent injunctive relief on the provisions
at issue here. App.427a–33a.
The RNC and Petersen  Petitioners asked the
Ninth Circuit to stay portions of the injunction , including the prohibition against enforcing the state -
form rejection provision . This Court ultimately
granted a stay as to the state-form rejection provision.
App.426a. No party sought to stay the injunction as to
the registration-cancellation provisions.
After full briefing and oral argument, the Ninth
Circuit affirmed the relevant portions of the district
court’s permanent injunction. Like the district court,
the panel concluded that the LULAC Consent Decree
and NVRA each independently prohibit  enforcement
of the state -form rejection provision . App.47a–52a.
The court explained that consent decrees have the effect of a “binding final judgment [] that remain[s] in

10


force” absent an approved request for modification or
vacatur. App.47a. Arizona could not, via state legislation, compel the State’s election officials “to enforce
legislation contrary to the final judgment of [a] federal
decree.” App.48a–49a. The court further held that the
NVRA does not permit Arizona to require documentary proof of citizenship from state form applicants for
federal elections. App.50a–52a.
The court also held that H.B. 2243 violate d the
NVRA to the extent it “authorizes systematic cancellation of registrations [of alleged noncitizens] within
90 days before a federal election.” App.47a. Its systematic cancellation scheme was  “precisely the type of
systematic cancellation program that the 90-day Provision was meant to preclude.” App.46a.
The Ninth Circuit denied Petitioners’ petitions for
rehearing en banc. This Court granted the petition for
certiorari on June 29, 2026.
SUMMARY OF THE ARGUMENT
1. The Ninth Circuit correctly held that the NVRA
prohibits Arizona from rejecting applicants using its
state form to register for federal elections when those
applicants do not provide documentary proof of citizenship. Arizona may require state form applicants to
provide documentary proof of citizenship when registering for state and local elections, but for federal elections, the NVRA provides that the state form can require “only such” information that is “necessary.” 52
U.S.C. § 20508(b)(1). Arizona is barred from requiring
federal form applicants to provide documentary proof

11


of citizenship when registering to vote for federal elections, so it follows that such documentation is not
“necessary” for state form applicants seeking to register to vote for federal elections. The Ninth Circuit correctly reached that determination a fter holding that
“necessary,” as used in §  20508(b)(1), should receive
its ordinary meaning of “essential.” The Court should
adopt that construction too . But Petitioners failed to
establish that documentary proof of citizenship is
“necessary” under any definition of the term—indeed,
they made no factual showing at all. That in itself requires affirmance. But if the Court disagrees, it
should, at most, remand for fact finding on the issue.
2. The Ninth Circuit correctly held, in the alternative, that a never -challenged consent decree also requires Arizona to accept state form applications without documentary proof of citizenship for purposes of
federal elections. Petitioner s had ample opportunity
to seek to modify or set aside that consent decree, but
they chose instead to ignore it. That cannot be sufficient. A consent decree is a binding judgment from a
federal court; pretending that it does not exist does
not diminish its effect on the parties bound by it. And
because Petitioners have not tried going to the issuing
court to seek relief from judgment, this case presents
no legitimate concerns about executive officials binding the hands of state legislatures.
3. The Ninth Circuit also correctly held that the
NVRA requires Arizona to pause its program to systematically remove voters flagged by databases as
possible noncitizens for the 90 days leading up to a
federal election. Arizona has many other avenues to

12


remove noncitizens on its rolls—it can do so systematically at any time outside the 90-day period before an
election, and it can do so on an individualized basis
even on the eve of an election. But the NVRA requires
that “any program” to systematically  remove voters
from the rolls stop when federal elections draw  near.
Id. § 20507(c)(2)(A). The NVRA contains no exception
for removals targeting potential noncitizens, and Petitioners’ attempts to shoehorn such an exception into
the NVRA fail as a matter of plain text and according
to well- worn rules of statutory interpretation. Petitioners’ repeated accusation that this result runs to
the benefit of noncitizens ineligible to vote fundamentally misunderstands the NVRA. The point of the 90 -
day provision is not to protect ineligible voters from
removal but to protect eligible voters from being mistakenly swept up in a removal program —a remarkably common and well -documented occurrence when
databases are used to identify potential noncitizens .
While such errors may be fixable in due course, that
is often not so shortly before an election . The 90-day
provision reflects Congress’s effort to protect eligible
voters from such disenfranchisement —a risk that is
no less present when a program flags voters as suspected noncitizens rather than as potential nonresidents. The Ninth Circuit’s decision accords with the
two other circuits that have addressed this issue and
preserves the vital protections Congress wrote into
the NVRA to protect eligible voters from erroneous removals.

13


ARGUMENT
I. The NVRA does not allow Arizona to categorically reject state form  applicants
without documentary proof of citizenship.
The NVRA requires States to “accept and use” the
federal form promulgated by the EAC for registration
to vote in federal elections, while providing that
States also “may develop and use” their own state
forms for that purpose. 52 U.S.C. § 20505(a). Exactly
the same statutory standard applies to what information both forms may request, however: “only such
identifying information . . . and other information . . .
as is necessary to enable the appropriate State election official to as sess the eligibility of the applicant
and to administer voter registration and other parts
of the elect ion process.” Id. § 20508(b)(1); see id.
§ 20505(a)(2).
The EAC is tasked with applying the NVRA’s “necessary” standard for purposes of the federal form, id.
§ 20508(a), and it has found that documentary proof
of citizenship is not “necessary” under the statutory
standard—a finding upheld by courts. See Kobach,
772 F.3d 1183. This Court has held that, absent the
EAC requiring documentary proof of citizenship with
the federal form, Arizona cannot require documentary
proof of citizenship from voters who register using
that form. See ITCA, 570 U.S. at 15. It is therefore undisputed that if a voter submits a federal form without
documentary proof of citizenship, the NVRA requires
Arizona to register that voter for federal elections.

14


This case is limited to the state form that Arizona

A consent decree entered by an Article III court
acts as “a final judgment” and is “enforceable as, a judicial decree that is subject to the rules generally applicable to other judgments and decrees.”  Rufo v. Inmates of Suffolk Cnty. Jail , 502 U.S. 367, 378, 391

time. Thus, like any other final judgment, a consent

grant enduring relief that materially alters the legal
relationship between the parties.” Lackey, 604 U.S. at

That does not mean a consent decree is set in
stone. Federal courts retain authority to revisit consent judgments as part of their innate equitable jurisdiction, upon which consent decrees with prospective
effect depend. Milk Wagon Drivers Union v. Meadowmoor Dairies, 312 U.S. 287, 298 (1941) (Frankfurter, J.) (“Familiar equity procedure assures opportunity for modifying or vacating an injunction when
its continuance is no longer warranted”); see also N.Y.
State Ass’n for Retarded Child. Inc. v. Carey, 706 F.2d
956, 967 (2d Cir. 1983) (Friendly, J.) (“The power of a
court of equity to modify a decree of injunctive relief
